evidence.claim: Marble’s quarries sent most of their stone out as cemetery headstones across nine states.
evidence.quote: The vast majority of all marble quarried in the communty was used as cemetery headstones across nine states.

evidence.claim: They opened in 1902, shipping Regal Blue and Confederate Gray marble on the Southern Railway’s Murphy Branch.
evidence.quote: The quarries opened in 1902 and produced Regal Blue and Confederate Gray shades which were shipped on the Southern Railway's Murphy Branch.

evidence.claim: The stone also went into the Cherokee County Courthouse, built in 1926 and constructed entirely of marble.
evidence.quote: The Cherokee County Courthouse, built in 1926, was the first building made of marble from the community. It is one of few county courthouses in the U.S. constructed entirely of marble.

evidence.claim: By 1946, heavy water flow and excessive jointing had closed all but one quarry.
evidence.quote: By 1946, all but one quarry in the community had closed due to excessive jointing and heavy water flow.

evidence.claim: None now operates, and all have filled with water. The community’s former name, Marble Springs, survives in the name of its Baptist church on Marble Road.
evidence.quote: Currently, none are functioning, and all have filled with water.

evidence.claim: The community’s former name, Marble Springs, survives in the name of its Baptist church on Marble Road.
evidence.quote: The original name of the Marble community is Marble Springs. The name was later shortened to Marble with the baptist church on Marble Road still bearing the original name.

evidence.claim: At Wesser, the lower rafting run meets a former railway whistle stop.
evidence.quote: At one time, Wesser was a whistle stop for the Southern Railway on the Murphy Branch.

evidence.claim: The eight-mile run from the Nantahala Powerhouse to Wesser has Class II and III rapids.
evidence.quote: The part that can be rafted is 8 miles (13 km) long and has Class II and III rapids. It extends from the Nantahala Powerhouse to the town of Wesser.

evidence.claim: Its water depends on releases from Nantahala Lake: water diverted through a 5.5-mile penstock passes through the powerhouse before returning to the river channel.
evidence.quote: The Nantahala dam is a diversion dam; the water that normally flows through the river is diverted through a 5.5-mile (8.9 km) penstock before flowing through the Nantahala Powerhouse and back into the original river channel far downstream.

evidence.claim: Beyond the main take-out, Lower Nantahala Falls, also called Wesser Falls, drops at about 45 degrees among sharp rocks.
evidence.quote: Just beyond the main take-out point in Wesser lies Lower Nantahala Falls, or Wesser Falls, which drops off at about a 45-degree angle with many sharp rocks.

evidence.claim: Excursion trains on the Great Smoky Mountains Railroad stop in Wesser.
evidence.quote: The Great Smoky Mountains Railroad stops here during excursions.

evidence.claim: Its water depends on releases from Nantahala Lake
evidence.quote: The flow rate of this section of the Nantahala is dependent on releases from Nantahala Lake

evidence.claim: Main and Everett streets preserve the T-shaped layout of a county seat first called Charleston.
evidence.quote: Initially known as Charleston, the county seat was laid out in a T-shape, formed by what are now Main and Everett streets

evidence.claim: The town changed its name to Bryson City in 1889 to recognize Thaddeus Bryson’s part in its development and avoid confusion with Charleston, South Carolina.
evidence.quote: In 1889, the people of Charleston changed the city's name to "Bryson City" to acknowledge the role of Thaddeus Bryson in its development, and to eliminate confusion from sharing a name with Charleston, South Carolina.

evidence.claim: Southern Railway’s depot followed in 1895, a frame building with broad eaves and wooden ornament.
evidence.quote: A frame building with wooden ornament and broad eaves was completed in 1895.

evidence.claim: Passenger service ended in 1948. After North Carolina bought the Murphy Branch in 1988, the station was refurbished for excursion passengers.
evidence.quote: On July 16, 1948, passenger rail service was discontinued along the Murphy Branch and the station was closed.

evidence.claim: Trains now depart for the Nantahala Gorge and Tuckasegee River.
evidence.quote: The train station, operated by the Great Smoky Mountains Railroad, provides round-trip excursions through the Nantahala Gorge and along the Tuckasegee River.

flags: NCDOT gives 47.2 miles; material gives 51.9 mapped miles and strip towns beyond that distance. Followed the guidebook’s Marble-to-US-74 endpoint via Highway 19A, beyond Bryson City; no claim that Bryson City is the terminus.

The 1839 Trail of Tears path claim is present in 16.txt, but no primary historical or Cherokee community source corroborates its precise corridor and date. Omitted under STYLE section 5, not treated as disproved.
NCDOT’s PDF extraction interleaves columns in its directions. Driving sequence was checked against named road segments and strip-town order; no turn-by-turn navigation is supplied.

Current moment facts are cache-supported. Kituwa and the Tsali/Yonaguska monuments were omitted to focus the Bryson City narrative on the town layout and depot, not for lack of cache evidence. No current moment was dropped.
The guidebook is dated 2021. Its drive time is presented as a guidebook figure; obsolete train hours and seasonal service guarantees are omitted.
